title: The light of the world (John 8:12–30)
hook: whoever follows me won't walk in darkness
tomorrow: the truth will set you free

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman dragged into the middle, words written in the dust, and stones dropped one by one. Your line was neither do I condemn you. Did you set a stone down? Day six hundred fifteen.

Jerusalem had no streetlights. After sunset there were oil lamps, the moon, and not much else. Then, one week a year, the temple lights up. According to the Mishnah, during the Feast of Tabernacles, huge golden lampstands stood in the temple's Court of the Women, each with bowls of oil, and young priests climbed ladders to fill them. Wicks were made from the priests' worn-out garments. The tradition says there wasn't a courtyard in Jerusalem that wasn't lit by that light. People danced with torches beneath it all night. And in that same court, Jesus speaks.

"I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life." This is the second of the I am sayings in John. Bread first, now light. And John tells us exactly where he said it: "These words spake Jesus in the treasury, as he taught in the temple." The treasury, where the offering chests stood, was in the Court of the Women, the same court where those great lamps burned at the feast. So picture him there, near the lampstands, saying: I am the light. Light has run through John's Gospel since its first lines. John's first lines said the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness could not grasp it or put it out. Now the light speaks for itself. Notice the shape of the promise. He doesn't say, whoever follows me will never face darkness. Night still comes. He says, they won't walk in darkness. They'll carry the light of life with them, like someone walking home at night with a lamp. The path isn't lit all the way to the end; just enough for the next step. The people listening push back. You're testifying about yourself; that doesn't count. Jesus answers that his Father bears witness with him. Who are you? they ask. And he speaks of a day when they'll lift up the Son of Man, a hint of the cross, and then they'll know. John ends this scene simply: as he spoke these words, many believed in him.
screen: then, large: `I AM THE LIGHT OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk somewhere lit, slowly. If you can, stand and walk slowly toward a window or a lamp. If you can't move right now, turn toward the brightest thing in the room. Settle, and breathe. Let your eyes rest on the light. Notice how it falls on things, how it shows you the floor, the edges, the way forward. Take a few slow steps, or simply breathe slowly, and notice you only need enough light for the next step. If you pray, you can ask for light on one part of your path. If you don't, rest in the brightness. The bell holds the time.
The light of the world. The second of Jesus's I am sayings in John, spoken in the temple where the great festival lamps burned.

segments.voice: Your line: the light of life. Today, when you switch on a light, pause for a second and ask what the next step is. Just the next one. Day six hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Many Christians light candles in worship as a sign of Christ as the light of the world; at the Easter Vigil in many churches, a single candle is carried into a dark church and its flame is shared.

original.note: Greek: light. The same word John uses in his first chapter: the light shines in the darkness.

trapdoor: what you thought: a general saying about Jesus being good and bright.
what it means: in the court where festival lamps lit the city, Jesus says he is the light for everyone, enough for the next step.
what a scholar hears: the Mishnah describes golden lampstands in the Court of the Women at Sukkot, and John places this saying in the treasury there.

notes: Lamp-lighting at Sukkot: Mishnah Sukkah 5:2–4 (golden lampstands, youths of the priestly stock with ladders, wicks from priests' worn garments, every courtyard lit, torch dances). Confirm details.
The location of the treasury in the Court of the Women is the common scholarly view; confirm.
John 1:5 paraphrased ('the darkness has not overcome it'): KJV reads 'comprehended it not'. Not marked as quotation; confirm acceptable.
Whether John 8:12 continues the Tabernacles setting after the inserted 7:53–8:11 is the usual reading; confirm.

Audit (second sample): the teach's echo of John 1:5 used modern-translation wording ('has not overcome it', RSV/NRSV style) as if quoting; now a plain paraphrase matching day 592's grasp/overpower reading. Hook no longer opens with the templated 'Imagine'.
